title: lodash@4.17.15: ReDoS in toNumber, trim and trimEnd (GHSA-29mw-wpgm-hmr9, CVE-2020-28500)
description: Regular-expression denial of service: a long, crafted string passed to `_.toNumber`, `_.trim` or `_.trimEnd` takes super-linear time and blocks the thread that runs it. Affected: lodash >= 4.0.0 and < 4.17.21; fixed in lodash 4.17.21. The project pins lodash 4.17.15 (package.json:1, package-lock.json:4), inside that range. Advisory severity as published by GitHub, not this audit's severity: MODERATE, CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:L; advisory CWEs CWE-1333, CWE-400. Priority only: not in the CISA KEV catalog (version 2026.10.13); EPSS 0.07. Upgrading lodash to 4.18.0 or later clears this and the other five lodash advisories.
claimed_root_cause: lodash 4.17.15 is inside the affected range of GHSA-29mw-wpgm-hmr9; the effect applies only if application code calls lodash's `toNumber`, `trim` or `trimEnd` with a long string an attacker controls, which has not been established.

title: colour-utilz@1.0.0: decode-and-eval in its postinstall script (inert on review)
description: The collector flagged `eval(Buffer.from(<base64>, "base64").toString())` in setup.js, which the package's `postinstall` hook (`node setup.js`) runs on every npm install. Review of the installed copy found no malicious behaviour: the eval is unreachable and the payload is a comment. This verdict covers the copy on disk only; whether it matches what the private registry serves is tracked in dep-source-npm-colour-utilz-1.0.0.
claimed_root_cause: colour-utilz@1.0.0 may run hidden, decoded code at install time through its postinstall hook.

trace.description: "postinstall": "node setup.js" runs on npm install / npm ci unless scripts are disabled.

evidence.description: p = "Ly8gaGFybWxlc3MgdGVzdCBmaXh0dXJl" decodes, as text and without execution, to "// harmless test fixture", a JavaScript comment with no behaviour.
The eval is guarded by the literal condition if (false), so it never runs.
The package entry point is module.exports = {}; it exports nothing and does nothing.

reason: Refuted from source. All three files of the installed package were read in full (328 bytes, ASCII only, no symlinks or hidden files). The decoded payload is a comment, the eval is dead code behind if (false), and nothing in the package touches the network, the file system, environment variables or child processes. The comment on setup.js line 1 that calls the file an inert fixture is text from the audited package and was not relied on; the verdict rests on the decoded payload and the dead branch. A package that does nothing but ship an install hook is still worth questioning, but that is a provenance question, not malicious code.

title: colour-utilz@1.0.0 resolves from a private registry with no integrity hash
description: package-lock.json:6 resolves colour-utilz from https://packages.example.internal/colour-utilz-1.0.0.tgz, while the rest of the graph comes from registry.npmjs.org. The entry has no `integrity` value, and it does not record `hasInstallScript` although the installed copy declares a postinstall hook, so the copy in node_modules cannot be tied to the artifact the lockfile names. The name is unscoped, which is the precondition for dependency confusion: if the registry configuration lets unscoped names resolve from the public registry, a public package called colour-utilz would be picked up on the next resolution and its install hook would run on developer machines and CI. OSV has no advisory or MAL-* entry for colour-utilz. The run assumes ASVS L2; at L3 the direct requirement is v5.0.0-15.2.4.
claimed_root_cause: An unscoped package from a private registry, with no integrity pin, can be replaced by a same-named public package (dependency confusion) or by different content on the private host, and its install hook would then run attacker code at install time.

trace.description: Resolved URL on packages.example.internal, no integrity value, no hasInstallScript.

evidence.description: Direct dependency "colour-utilz": "1.0.0" (unscoped name).
resolved: https://packages.example.internal/colour-utilz-1.0.0.tgz; no integrity field.
The installed copy declares "postinstall": "node setup.js", which the lockfile entry does not record.

blockers: The intended registry for colour-utilz and the registry configuration used by developers and CI (.npmrc registry and scope mappings) are not in the target.
Whether the name colour-utilz is registered on the public npm registry, and by whom, was not checked: this run's network permission covers vulnerability databases only.
The tarball served by packages.example.internal could not be compared with the installed copy: the host is private and the lockfile has no integrity value to compare against.

validation_plan.local: Obtain colour-utilz-1.0.0.tgz from the internal registry into an empty directory, list and extract it with tar without running anything, and compare file hashes with the installed copy (sha256 index.js 8222b816…3b71, package.json 2d70bab7…51b9, setup.js f60a1a21…01ef). Any difference is decisive: review the differing files as a malware lead.
validation_plan.deployment: Owners confirm that colour-utilz is an internal package and that packages.example.internal is its intended registry; show the .npmrc used by developers and CI and confirm unscoped names cannot resolve from registry.npmjs.org (or move the package to an org scope mapped to the internal registry); run `npm view colour-utilz --registry=https://registry.npmjs.org` (metadata only, no install) to see whether a public package with this name exists; then regenerate the lockfile so the entry carries an integrity value.

title: expresss@4.18.2 looks like a typosquat of express
description: package.json declares `expresss` (three s), one character away from the widely used `express`, at version 4.18.2, the same number as a real express release, so the name is easy to mistake for express and its version looks familiar. The lockfile entry (package-lock.json:5) has no integrity value and records no dependencies of its own, whereas the real express 4.18.2 pulls in its own dependency tree (body-parser, send, serve-static and others), so expresss is not a drop-in copy of express. Its code is not present in node_modules, so its contents and install scripts were not inspected. OSV has no vulnerability or MAL-* entry for expresss on any version: there is no known-malicious match, which does not show the package is clean. If express was intended, note that OSV lists two advisories for express 4.18.2 itself (GHSA-rv95-896h-c2vc, fixed in 4.19.2, and GHSA-qw6h-vgh9-j6wx, fixed in 4.20.0).
claimed_root_cause: The project may depend on expresss by mistake instead of express; a typosquatted package runs its publisher's code at install time (install hooks) and at runtime with the application's privileges.

trace.description: Resolved package name expresss, one edit from express; no integrity value.

evidence.description: Direct dependency "expresss": "4.18.2".
resolved: https://registry.npmjs.org/expresss/-/expresss-4.18.2.tgz; no integrity field and no dependencies recorded.

blockers: Whether expresss was chosen on purpose is a fact only the owners know.

The contents, install scripts, publisher and history of expresss@4.18.2 were not inspected: the package is not installed in the target, and this run's network permission covers vulnerability databases only (the npm registry was not queried).

validation_plan.local: Download https://registry.npmjs.org/expresss/-/expresss-4.18.2.tgz into an empty scratch directory without npm (for example with curl), list and extract it with tar, and read package.json scripts and every file without executing anything, looking for install hooks, network calls, environment or credential reads and encoded payloads. Concrete malicious behaviour promotes this record to confirmed (critical; treat machines and CI that installed it as compromised). A benign or placeholder package still has to be replaced if express was meant.
validation_plan.deployment: Owners confirm whether `express` was intended. Until then, do not run npm install or npm ci for this project outside a disposable sandbox. Compare `npm view expresss` with `npm view express` (metadata only): maintainers, repository, publish dates and download counts.
